# The Handler Contract

Handlers are shell adapters: they map parsed CLI input to application calls and
return serializable CLI-owned view data. Keep reusable behavior in a CLI-free
library. The handler contract is designed to be **explicit** rather than
permissive, so adapters remain testable and decoupled from output formatting.

---

## Quick Start: The `#[handler]` Macro

For most handlers, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed adapter functions:

```rust,ignore
use standout_macros::handler;

#[handler]
pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[arg] limit: Option<usize>) -> Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error> {
    storage::list(all, limit)
}
```

The macro leaves `list` alone and adds three items beside it:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | reads the arguments out of `ArgMatches` and calls `list`. It returns **the annotated return type verbatim** — here `Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error>`, not `HandlerResult<Vec<Item>>` |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `App::verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing [`Handler`](#the-handler-trait) — **the registrable item** |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `list_Handler`'s
`Handler::handle`, which calls `IntoHandlerResult::into_handler_result` on
whatever `list__handler` returned. It is not applied by `list__handler` itself.
Only registration of `list_Handler` runs that wrap. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` does
not reach the trait object at all: it registers the closure
`handlers::list__handler` through `GroupBuilder::command_with`, so nothing
calls `Handler::handle` and the annotated return type has to be a
`HandlerResult` shape already. That is the difference the next two tables
spell out.

The un-suffixed `handlers::list` is not registrable — it has the wrong
signature by design, so that a test can call it directly. Which of the other
two items you register depends on the method:

| Method | What it takes | What to pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AppBuilder::command_with` | `impl Handler` | `handlers::list_Handler` |
| `GroupBuilder::command` / `command_with`, and therefore `#[derive(Dispatch)]` | a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>` | `handlers::list__handler` |

That second row constrains the return type, and it is the one place the two
registration paths genuinely differ. `list__handler` returns the annotated type
verbatim, so it satisfies `HandlerResult<T>` only when the function was written
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` (or `-> Result<(), E>`, whose wrapper returns
`HandlerResult<()>`). **A handler annotated `-> Result<T, E>` cannot be
registered through `#[derive(Dispatch)]`**: expansion fails with `expected
list__handler to return Result<Output<_>, Error>, but it returns Result<Items,
Error>`. Write it `-> Result<Output<T>, E>`, or register `list_Handler` through
`AppBuilder::command_with`, where `Handler::handle` applies the wrap for you.

The three return shapes, and the original functions still being callable:

```rust
use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Output};
use standout::handler;

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Items {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; `handle` wraps the value in `Output::Render`.
#[handler]
pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Items, anyhow::Error> {
    let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
    if all {
        names.push("cron".to_string());
    }
    Ok(Items { names })
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; the `Output` passes through untouched.
#[handler]
pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Items>, anyhow::Error> {
    Ok(Output::Render(Items { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `()`; `handle` produces `Output::Silent`.
#[handler]
pub fn reload(#[flag] _force: bool) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    // No ArgMatches, no dispatcher: the annotated function is what a unit test calls.
    assert_eq!(list(true).unwrap().names, ["ssh", "cron"]);
    reload(false).unwrap();
}
```

Every `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` attribute is listed in the
[`#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` reference](../../../topics/dispatch-attributes.md).

**Parameter Annotations:**

| Annotation            | Type              | Extraction                    |
| --------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `#[flag]`             | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("name")`    |
| `#[flag(name = "x")]` | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("x")`       |
| `#[arg]`              | `T`               | Required argument             |
| `#[arg]`              | `Option<T>`       | Optional argument             |
| `#[arg]`              | `Vec<T>`          | Multiple values               |
| `#[arg(name = "x")]`  | `T`               | Argument with custom CLI name |
| `#[ctx]`              | `&CommandContext` | Access to context             |
| `#[matches]`          | `&ArgMatches`     | Raw matches (escape hatch)    |

Without `name = "x"`, the argument id is the parameter name with underscores
turned into hyphens: `no_legend` reads the argument id `no-legend`. Clap's own
derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so a clap-derive
`no_legend` field declares `#[arg(id = "no-legend")]` to meet the handler, or
the handler parameter takes the field's id with `#[flag(name = "no_legend")]`.
`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch instead of leaving it to a
runtime `get_flag` panic. A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the
`r#` first, the way clap's derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads
the argument id `type`.

**Return Type Handling:** the function must return `Result<T, E>`; the macro
rejects anything else with `handler must return Result<T, E>`. What `T` is
decides what `Handler::Output` becomes and whether anything is wrapped.

| Annotated return type | `Handler::Output` | What `handle` produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Result<T, E>` | `T` | `Ok(value)` wrapped in `Output::Render(value)` |
| `Result<Output<T>, E>` (that is, `HandlerResult<T>`) | `T` | the `Output` you returned, unchanged |
| `Result<(), E>` | `()` | `Output::Silent` |

> **Testing:** The original function is preserved, so you can test directly: `list(true, Some(10))`.

---

## The Handler Trait

```rust,ignore
pub trait Handler {
    type Output: Serialize;
    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Self::Output>;
}
```

Key characteristics:

- **Mutable self**: `&mut self` allows direct state modification
- **Output must be Serialize**: Needed for JSON/YAML modes and template context

Implementing the trait directly is useful when your handler needs internal state—database connections, configuration, caches, etc.

### Example: Struct Handler with State

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
use clap::ArgMatches;
use serde::Serialize;

struct CachingDatabase {
    connection: Connection,
    cache: HashMap<String, Vec<Row>>,
}

impl CachingDatabase {
    fn query_with_cache(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Vec<Row>, Error> {
        if let Some(cached) = self.cache.get(sql) {
            return Ok(cached.clone());
        }
        let result = self.connection.execute(sql)?;
        self.cache.insert(sql.to_string(), result.clone());
        Ok(result)
    }
}

impl Handler for CachingDatabase {
    type Output = Vec<Row>;

    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
        let rows = self.query_with_cache(query)?;  // &mut self works!
        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
    }
}
```

---

## Closure Handlers

Most handlers are simple closures using `FnHandler`:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{FnHandler, Output, HandlerResult};

let mut counter = 0;

let handler = FnHandler::new(move |_matches, _ctx| {
    counter += 1;  // Mutation works!
    Ok(Output::Render(counter))
});
```

The closure signature:

```rust,ignore
fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>
where T: Serialize
```

Closures are `FnMut`, allowing captured variables to be mutated.

---

## SimpleFnHandler (No Context Needed)

When your handler doesn't need `CommandContext`, use `SimpleFnHandler` for a cleaner signature:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::SimpleFnHandler;

let handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|matches| {
    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(ListResult { items, verbose })
});
```

The closure signature:

```rust,ignore
fn(&ArgMatches) -> Result<T, E>
where T: Serialize, E: Into<anyhow::Error>
```

`SimpleFnHandler` automatically wraps the result in `Output::Render` via `IntoHandlerResult`.

---

## IntoHandlerResult Trait

The `IntoHandlerResult` trait enables handlers to return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `HandlerResult<T>`:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::IntoHandlerResult;

// Before: explicit Output wrapping
fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}

// After: automatic conversion
fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> impl IntoHandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    storage::list()  // Result<Vec<Item>, Error> auto-converts
}
```

The trait is implemented for:

- `Result<T, E>` where `E: Into<anyhow::Error>` → wraps `Ok(t)` in `Output::Render(t)`
- `HandlerResult<T>` → passes through unchanged

This is used internally by `SimpleFnHandler` and the `#[handler]` macro.

---

## HandlerResult

`HandlerResult<T>` is a standard `Result` type:

```rust,ignore
pub type HandlerResult<T> = Result<Output<T>, anyhow::Error>;
```

The `?` operator works naturally for error propagation:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Items> {
    let items = storage::load()?;           // Propagates errors
    let filtered = filter_items(&items)?;   // Propagates errors
    Ok(Output::Render(Items { filtered }))
}
```

### Authoritative external failures

When a handler delegates to another executable and the application's contract
requires that executable's exact nonzero status and stderr, return the public
`ExternalFailure` type through the same `HandlerResult` seam:

```rust,ignore
let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, git_stderr)?;
Err(failure.into())
```

Construction rejects status `0`. Standout recognizes only this concrete type,
preserves its diagnostic verbatim, and exposes it as `RunErrorKind::External`.
Ordinary handler errors still use status `1`; this is not a general exit-code
mapping mechanism. Handlers must not print or call `process::exit` themselves.

---

## The Output Enum

`Output<T>` represents what a handler produces:

```rust,ignore
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
    Render(T),
    Silent,
    Binary { data: Vec<u8>, filename: String },
    Artifact(Artifact<T>),
}
```

`Output` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: matches on it need a `_` arm so later shapes
can be added without breaking downstream code.

### Output::Render(T)

The common case. Data is passed to the render function:

```rust,ignore
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListResult {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
        total: items.len(),
        items,
    }))
}
```

### Output::Silent

No output produced. Useful for commands with side effects only:

```rust,ignore
fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
    storage::delete(id)?;
    Ok(Output::Silent)
}
```

Silent behavior:

- Post-output hooks still receive `RenderedOutput::Silent`
- Render function is not called
- Nothing prints to stdout

### Output::Binary

Raw bytes for file output:

```rust,ignore
fn export_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
    let data = generate_report()?;
    let pdf_bytes = render_to_pdf(&data)?;

    Ok(Output::Binary {
        data: pdf_bytes,
        filename: "report.pdf".into(),
    })
}
```

Binary output bypasses the render function entirely.

The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not permission to write. Without
`--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to stdout and touches no file. If
you want the framework to write the suggested destination, use `Output::Artifact`
— that opt-in is the whole difference between the two shapes.

### Output::Artifact

Owned bytes plus an application-owned report, for commands that produce a file
*and* have something to say about it. `Output::Binary` cannot carry a report,
and nothing renders after its write, so a command that wants to say "exported 12
rows to /tmp/report.csv (2 warnings)" would otherwise have to write the file
itself — pulling destination policy back into the application core.

```rust,ignore
use standout::cli::{Artifact, HandlerResult, Output};

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ExportReport {
    exported: usize,
    warnings: Vec<Warning>,
}

fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ExportReport> {
    let export = core::export_csv()?;   // bytes + facts, no filesystem

    Ok(Output::Artifact(
        Artifact::new(export.csv)
            .suggest_destination(export.suggested_filename)
            .with_report(ExportReport {
                exported: export.rows,
                warnings: export.warnings,
            }),
    ))
}
```

Who owns what:

| Concern | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| Artifact bytes | Application |
| Suggested destination | Application (a suggestion) |
| Semantic report and warning taxonomy | Application |
| Destination selection | Framework |
| The write and its failure | Framework |
| Receipt (completed destination) | Framework |

#### Destination policy

Standout selects the destination deterministically:

1. the explicit `--output-file-path` override;
2. the artifact's `suggest_destination(...)`, if the application opted in;
3. stdout, if the application opted in with `allow_stdout()`.

If none applies, the run fails with `FinalWrite(Artifact)` rather than inventing
a file or dropping the bytes. All three steps share that one failure path.

#### Write first, report second

Standout writes, then renders the report from a fixed envelope:

```json
{
  "report": { "exported": 12, "warnings": [] },
  "receipt": { "destination": "/tmp/report.csv", "stdout": false, "byte_count": 480 }
}
```

So a template can say what only the framework knows:

```jinja
Exported {{ report.exported }} rows to {{ receipt.destination }}
```

The envelope shape is fixed (`report` + `receipt`) whatever the report's type,
so no application key can collide with the receipt. Structured modes serialize
the same envelope. A failed write renders nothing: success cannot outrun the
write that justifies it.

#### The report channel

Mixing a report into the bytes would corrupt them, so the channel follows the
destination:

| Artifact destination | Report goes to |
| --- | --- |
| File | stdout |
| Stdout (`allow_stdout()`) | stderr |

#### Hooks and artifacts

Post-dispatch hooks see the report as ordinary handler data. Post-output hooks
see `RenderedOutput::Artifact` and can still transform the bytes or the report
via `as_artifact_mut()`. Hooks never perform the write — that stays framework-
owned, which is what keeps the failure path single and the report honest.

Bytes are owned; streaming is deliberately not part of this contract.

---

## CommandContext

`CommandContext` provides execution environment information and state access:

```rust,ignore
pub struct CommandContext {
    pub command_path: Vec<String>,
    pub app_state: Rc<Extensions>,
    pub extensions: Extensions,
}
```

**command_path**: The subcommand chain as a vector, e.g., `["db", "migrate"]`. Useful for logging or conditional logic.

**app_state**: Shared, immutable state configured at app build time via `AppBuilder::app_state()`. Wrapped in `Arc` for cheap cloning. Use for database connections, configuration, API clients.

**extensions**: Per-request, mutable state injected by pre-dispatch hooks. Use for user sessions, request IDs, computed values.

> For comprehensive coverage of state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).

---

## State Access: App State vs Extensions

Handlers access state through two distinct mechanisms with different semantics:

| Aspect         | `ctx.app_state`               | `ctx.extensions`           |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| **Mutability** | Immutable (`&`)               | Mutable (`&mut`)           |
| **Lifetime**   | App lifetime                  | Per-request                |
| **Set by**     | `AppBuilder::app_state()`     | Pre-dispatch hooks         |
| **Use for**    | Database, Config, API clients | User sessions, request IDs |

### App State (Shared Resources)

Configure long-lived resources at build time:

```rust,ignore
App::builder()
    .app_state(Database::connect()?)
    .app_state(Config::load()?)
    .command("list", list_handler, template)?
    .build()?
```

Access in handlers via `ctx.app_state`:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
    let config = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Config>()?;

    let items = db.query_items(config.max_results)?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}
```

### Extensions (Per-Request State)

Pre-dispatch hooks inject request-scoped state:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};

struct UserScope { user_id: String, permissions: Vec<String> }

let hooks = Hooks::new()
    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
        // Can read app_state to set up per-request state
        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;

        let user_id = matches.get_one::<String>("user").unwrap().clone();
        let permissions = db.get_permissions(&user_id)?;

        ctx.extensions.insert(UserScope { user_id, permissions });
        Ok(())
    });
```

Handlers retrieve from extensions:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;       // shared
    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;  // per-request

    let items = db.list_for_user(&scope.user_id)?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}
```

### Extensions API

Both `app_state` and `extensions` use the same `Extensions` type with these methods:

| Method              | Description                                     |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `insert<T>(value)`  | Insert a value, returns previous if any         |
| `get<T>()`          | Get immutable reference, returns `Option<&T>`   |
| `get_required<T>()` | Get reference or return error if missing        |
| `get_mut<T>()`      | Get mutable reference, returns `Option<&mut T>` |
| `remove<T>()`       | Remove and return value                         |
| `contains<T>()`     | Check if type exists                            |
| `len()`             | Number of stored values                         |
| `is_empty()`        | True if no values stored                        |
| `clear()`           | Remove all values                               |

Use `get_required` for mandatory dependencies (fails fast with clear error), `get` for optional ones.

### When to Use Which

**Use App State for:**

- Database connections — expensive to create, should be pooled
- Configuration — loaded once at startup
- API clients — shared HTTP clients with connection pooling

**Use Extensions for:**

- User context — current user, session, permissions
- Request metadata — request ID, timing, correlation ID
- Transient state — data computed by one hook, used by handler

### The Two-State Pattern

The separation exists because:

1. **Closure capture doesn't work with `#[derive(Dispatch)]`** — macro-generated dispatch calls handlers with a fixed signature
2. **App-level resources shouldn't be created per-request** — database pools and config are expensive
3. **Per-request state needs mutable injection** — hooks compute values at runtime

```rust,ignore
// App state: configured once at build time
App::builder()
    .app_state(Database::connect()?)  // Shared via Arc
    .hooks("users.list", Hooks::new()
        .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
            // Extensions: computed per-request, can use app_state
            let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
            let user = authenticate(matches, db)?;
            ctx.extensions.insert(user);
            Ok(())
        }))?
```

> For comprehensive coverage of state management patterns, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).

---

## Accessing CLI Arguments

The `ArgMatches` parameter provides access to parsed arguments through clap's standard API:

```rust,ignore
fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Data> {
    // Flags
    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");

    // Required options
    let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();

    // Optional values
    let limit: Option<&u32> = matches.get_one("limit");

    // Multiple values
    let tags: Vec<&String> = matches.get_many("tags")
        .map(|v| v.collect())
        .unwrap_or_default();

    Ok(Output::Render(Data { ... }))
}
```

For subcommands, you work with the `ArgMatches` for your specific command level.

---

## Testing Handlers

Because handlers have explicit inputs and outputs, their adapter behavior is
straightforward to test directly. Test validation, filtering, and state
transitions through the CLI-free library instead:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_list_handler() {
    let cmd = Command::new("test")
        .arg(Arg::new("verbose").long("verbose").action(ArgAction::SetTrue));
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test", "--verbose"]).unwrap();

    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
        ..Default::default()
    };

    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);

    assert!(result.is_ok());
    if let Ok(Output::Render(data)) = result {
        assert!(data.verbose);
    }
}
```

No mocking frameworks needed—construct `ArgMatches` with clap, create a `CommandContext`, call your handler, assert on the result.

### Testing with App State

When handlers depend on app_state, inject test fixtures:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_handler_with_app_state() {
    use std::sync::Arc;

    // Create test fixtures
    let mock_db = MockDatabase::with_items(vec![
        Item { id: "1", name: "Test" }
    ]);

    // Build app_state with test data
    let mut app_state = Extensions::new();
    app_state.insert(mock_db);

    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
        app_state: Arc::new(app_state),
        extensions: Extensions::new(),
    };

    let cmd = Command::new("test");
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();

    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
    assert!(result.is_ok());
}
```

### Testing Handlers with Mutable State

Handler tests can verify state mutation across calls:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_handler_state_mutation() {
    struct Counter { count: u32 }

    impl Handler for Counter {
        type Output = u32;
        fn handle(&mut self, _m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<u32> {
            self.count += 1;
            Ok(Output::Render(self.count))
        }
    }

    let mut handler = Counter { count: 0 };
    let cmd = Command::new("test");
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["count".into()],
        ..Default::default()
    };

    // State accumulates across calls
    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
    let result = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);

    assert!(matches!(result, Ok(Output::Render(3))));
}
```

46	
47	- **I — Return data, not presentation.** A normal handler returns
48	  `Output::Render(data)`, `Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`. It
49	  should not print, emit ANSI, render a template, or branch on output mode.
50	- **I — Let the framework own the write for reported artifacts.** When a command
51	  produces a file *and* a report, return `Output::Artifact(...)` with owned bytes,
52	  an opt-in suggested destination, and the report. Standout selects the
53	  destination, writes, and renders the report afterwards with a receipt — the
54	  application never opens the file or words a success it hasn't earned.
55	- **I — Keep one data contract across modes.** `auto`, `term`, and `text` render
56	  the MiniJinja template and transform semantic style tags. `term-debug` keeps

64	  variant for the terminal background.

73	  style tags were placed, but it preserves known and unknown tags alike and
74	  does not validate that the tags exist. Use `validate_template` in development
75	  or tests to detect missing style definitions. Terminal mode's `?` marker is a
76	  visible warning, not a substitute for validation.
77	- **G — Do not imply integrated per-command CSV projection.** Normal app
78	  dispatch automatically flattens serializable data for CSV. The direct
79	  `render_auto_with_spec` API can render CSV with a `FlatDataSpec`, but arbitrary
80	  per-command projection through normal `App` dispatch is not currently
81	  integrated. Prefer a stable CLI-owned view DTO, or record the missing app
82	  configuration seam.

89	focused APIs and trade-offs.
90

92	
93	- **I — Core tests:** exercise validation, filtering, state transitions, and
94	  persistence through the CLI-free Rust interface.
95	- **I — Adapter tests:** call the typed handler function directly and assert the
96	  CLI-to-core mapping plus returned view DTO.
97	- **I — Pipeline tests:** use `standout-test::TestHarness` for Clap parsing,
98	  dispatch, hooks, inputs, templates, structured modes, and controlled process

100	- **A — Process tests:** reserve a small end-to-end layer for real PTYs,

102	  model.

113	  serialized-data transformation, or post-output observation at an explicit

119	- **Partial adoption** lets an existing Clap application delegate selected

Standout is most valuable when it creates a testable seam between application
behavior and shell presentation. Use this guide to review an implementation,
decide which framework capabilities add value, and name missing framework
support without pushing presentation concerns back into handlers.

## Evaluation classes

Classify every finding before deciding whether it needs work:

- **Invariant** — a property the application should preserve wherever Standout
  owns a command. Violating it weakens the architecture or public behavior.
- **Applicable capability** — a Standout feature that is valuable only when the
  application's needs call for it. Not using it is not automatically a defect.
- **Framework gap** — a desirable behavior that Standout does not currently
  integrate. Record the gap instead of hiding a custom workaround in a handler.

The checklist uses **I**, **A**, and **G** for those classes.

## Ownership and dispatch

- **I — Keep reusable behavior CLI-free.** Domain rules, state transitions,
  validation, persistence, and reusable services should expose ordinary Rust
  interfaces. A separate core crate is the recommended production shape, not a
  requirement enforced by Standout. Small applications may keep the same seam
  inside one crate.
- **I — Let the binary own the shell.** Clap types, Standout app construction,
  handlers, CLI view DTOs, templates, styles, environment lookup, and final
  output belong in the CLI package. Handlers are adapters: translate parsed
  arguments, call the core, and return serializable data.
- **I — Integrate with Clap.** Standout does not replace Clap. Clap remains the
  command and argument parser; Standout adds dispatch, rendering, output modes,
  hooks, and test seams around the resulting command model.
- **A — Prefer declarative dispatch when conventions fit.**
  `#[derive(Dispatch)]` maps Clap variants to handlers and can attach templates,
  hooks, nested dispatch, and pipes. Use explicit `command_with` registration
  when a command needs configuration that is clearer in builder code.

The production-shaped [`todo-core` + `tdoo` example](production-shaped-example.md)
shows this ownership boundary in executable code. The
[dispatch guide](../crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md) covers the
pipeline in detail.

## Output and rendering

- **I — Return data, not presentation.** A normal handler returns
  `Output::Render(data)`, `Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`. It
  should not print, emit ANSI, render a template, or branch on output mode.
- **I — Let the framework own the write for reported artifacts.** When a command
  produces a file *and* a report, return `Output::Artifact(...)` with owned bytes,
  an opt-in suggested destination, and the report. Standout selects the
  destination, writes, and renders the report afterwards with a receipt — the
  application never opens the file or words a success it hasn't earned.
- **I — Keep one data contract across modes.** `auto`, `term`, and `text` render
  the MiniJinja template and transform semantic style tags. `term-debug` keeps
  the tags visible. Structured `json`, `yaml`, `xml`, and `csv` modes serialize
  handler data directly and bypass templates, including template-injected
  context.
- **A — Use MiniJinja and semantic CSS.** Put layout in file-backed MiniJinja
  templates and appearance in CSS classes such as `.title` or `.warning`.
  Define adaptive overrides with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` and
  `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`; Standout resolves the matching style
  variant for the terminal background.
- **A — Embed resources and keep the debug loop short.** `embed_templates!` and
  `embed_styles!` provide release-safe assets. Hot reload specifically means
  that debug file-backed resources are re-read on render, so source edits can
  be observed without rebuilding while the original paths remain available.
- **A — Use tabular layout for column relationships.** Reach for the `col`
  filter and tabular specifications when alignment, width allocation,
  truncation, or nested columns matter; do not hand-pad strings in handlers.
- **I — Use the right render diagnostic.** `--output term-debug` shows where
  style tags were placed, but it preserves known and unknown tags alike and
  does not validate that the tags exist. Use `validate_template` in development
  or tests to detect missing style definitions. Terminal mode's `?` marker is a
  visible warning, not a substitute for validation.
- **G — Do not imply integrated per-command CSV projection.** Normal app
  dispatch automatically flattens serializable data for CSV. The direct
  `render_auto_with_spec` API can render CSV with a `FlatDataSpec`, but arbitrary
  per-command projection through normal `App` dispatch is not currently
  integrated. Prefer a stable CLI-owned view DTO, or record the missing app
  configuration seam.

See [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md),
[Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md),
[Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md),
[File System Resources](../crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md), and
[Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for the
focused APIs and trade-offs.

## Testing pyramid

- **I — Core tests:** exercise validation, filtering, state transitions, and
  persistence through the CLI-free Rust interface.
- **I — Adapter tests:** call the typed handler function directly and assert the
  CLI-to-core mapping plus returned view DTO.
- **I — Pipeline tests:** use `standout-test::TestHarness` for Clap parsing,
  dispatch, hooks, inputs, templates, structured modes, and controlled process
  seams. Mark harness tests serial because those seams are process-global.
- **A — Process tests:** reserve a small end-to-end layer for real PTYs,
  signals, subprocess behavior, and build or link boundaries the harness cannot
  model.

user-visible shell contract. See [Testing](../topics/testing.md) for the full
boundary matrix.

## Optional application capabilities

These are **applicable capabilities**, not baseline requirements:

- **Hooks** place cross-command validation, request-context injection,
  serialized-data transformation, or post-output observation at an explicit
  pipeline phase.
- **Declarative input chains** resolve values from arguments, environment,
  stdin, clipboard, defaults, editors, or prompts with one validation path.
- **Pipes** send or transform rendered text after output; binary and silent
  results pass through unchanged.
- **Partial adoption** lets an existing Clap application delegate selected
  commands to Standout and retain its legacy path for unmatched commands.

Adopt each capability only when it removes application-owned orchestration or
improves a test seam. If the framework cannot express the required behavior,
classify it as a framework gap and keep the workaround isolated in the CLI
layer.

## Review outcome

A high-quality implementation has no unresolved invariant violations, uses the
applicable capabilities that materially simplify its shell boundary, and names
framework gaps explicitly. That is a stronger signal than counting how many
Standout features an application uses.

1	# Standout How To
2	
3	This is a small, focused guide for adopting Standout in a working shell application. Each step is self-sufficient, takes a positive step towards a sane CLI design, and can be incrementally merged. This can be done for one command (probably a good idea), then replicated to as many as you'd like.
4	
5	Note that only 2 out of 8 steps are Standout related. The others are generally good practices and clear designs for maintainable shell programs. This is not an accident, as Standout's goal is to allow your app to keep a great structure effortlessly, while providing testability, rich and fast output design, and more.
6	
7	For explanation's sake, we will show a hypothetical list command for tdoo, a todo list manager.
8	
9	This guide keeps the migration in one package so each step is small. Once the
10	application behavior is separated from output, move it into a CLI-free library;
11	the canonical [production-shaped application](production-shaped-example.md)
12	shows the final ownership model.
13	
14	**See Also:**
15	
16	- [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) - detailed handler API
17	- [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) - dependency injection patterns
18	- [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) - themes and styles in depth
19	- [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md) - all output format options
20	- [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) - migrating incrementally
21	- [Input Collection](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) - declarative input from multiple sources
22	
23	## 1. Start: The Argument Parsing
24	
25	Arg parsing is insanely intricate and deceptively simple. In case you are not already: define your application's interface with clap. Nothing else is worth doing until you have a sane starting point.
26	
27	If you don't have clap set up yet, here's a minimal starting point:
28	
29	```rust
30	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
31	
32	#[derive(Parser)]
33	#[command(name = "tdoo")]
34	struct Cli {
35	    #[command(subcommand)]
36	    command: Commands,
37	}
38	
39	#[derive(Subcommand)]
40	enum Commands {
41	    /// List all todos
42	    List {
43	        #[arg(short, long)]
44	        all: bool,
45	    },
46	    /// Add a new todo
47	    Add {
48	        title: String,
49	    },
50	}
51	
52	fn main() {
53	    let cli = Cli::parse();
54	    match cli.command {
55	        Commands::List { all } => list_command(all),
56	        Commands::Add { title } => add_command(&title),
57	    }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	(If you are using a non-clap-compatible crate, for now, you'd have to write an adapter for clap.)
62	
63	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
64	
65	## 2. Hard Split Logic and Formatting
66	
67	Now, your command should be split into two functions: the logic handler and its rendering. Don't worry about the specifics, do the straightest path from your current code.
68	
69	This is the one key step, the key design rule. And that's not because Standout requires it, rather the other way around: Standout is designed on top of it, and keeping it separate and easy to iterate on both logic and presentation under this design is Standout's key value.
70	
71	If your CLI is in good shape this will be a small task, otherwise you may find yourself patching together print statements everywhere, tidying up the data model and centralizing the processing. The silver lining here being: if it takes considerable work, there will be considerable gain in doing so.
72	
73	**Before** (tangled logic and output):
74	
75	```rust
76	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
77	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
78	    println!("Your Todos:");
79	    println!("-----------");
80	    for (i, todo) in todos.iter().enumerate() {
81	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
82	            let marker = if todo.status == Status::Done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" };
83	            println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, marker, todo.title);
84	        }
85	    }
86	    if todos.is_empty() {
87	        println!("No todos yet!");
88	    }
89	}
90	```
91	
92	**After** (clean separation):
93	
94	```rust
95	use clap::ArgMatches;
96	
97	// Data types for your domain
98	#[derive(Clone)]
99	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
100	
101	#[derive(Clone)]
102	pub struct Todo {
103	    pub title: String,
104	    pub status: Status,
105	}
106	
107	pub struct TodoResult {
108	    pub message: Option<String>,
109	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
110	}
111	
112	// This is your application function. It knows nothing about clap and returns
113	// an ordinary Rust data type.
114	//
115	// Note: This example uses immutable references. If your application service
116	// needs mutable state (&mut self), see the "Mutable Handlers" section below.
117	pub fn list(show_done: bool) -> TodoResult {
118	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
119	
120	    let filtered: Vec<Todo> = if show_done {
121	        todos
122	    } else {
123	        todos.into_iter()
124	            .filter(|t| matches!(t.status, Status::Pending))
125	            .collect()
126	    };
127	
128	    TodoResult {
129	        message: None,
130	        todos: filtered,
131	    }
132	}
133	
134	// This will take the Rust data type and print the result to stdout
135	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
136	    if let Some(msg) = result.message {
137	        println!("{}", msg);
138	    }
139	    for (i, todo) in result.todos.iter().enumerate() {
140	        let status = match todo.status {
141	            Status::Done => "[x]",
142	            Status::Pending => "[ ]",
143	        };
144	        println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, status, todo.title);
145	    }
146	}
147	
148	// And the orchestrator:
149	pub fn list_command(matches: &ArgMatches) {
150	    render_list(list(matches.get_flag("all")))
151	}
152	```
153	
154	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` and then `tdoo list` - output should look identical to before.
155	
156	### Intermezzo A: Milestone - Logic and Presentation Split
157	
158	**What you achieved:** Your command logic is now a pure function that returns data.
159	**What's now possible:**
160	
161	- All of your app's logic can be unit tested as any code, from the logic inwards.
162	- You can test by passing domain inputs directly to the application function.
163	- The rendering can also be tested by feeding data inputs and matching outputs (though this is brittle).
164	
165	**What's next:** Making the return type serializable for automatic JSON/YAML output.
166	**Your files now:**
167	
168	```text
169	src/
170	├── main.rs          # clap setup + orchestrators
171	├── core.rs          # list(), add() - CLI-free application behavior
172	└── render.rs        # render_list(), render_add() - output formatting
173	```
174	
175	## 3. Fine Tune the Application Result Type
176	
177	While any data type works, Standout's renderer takes a generic type that must implement `Serialize`. This enables automatic JSON/YAML output modes and template rendering through MiniJinja's context system. This is likely a small change, and beneficial as a baseline for logic results that will simplify writing renderers later.
178	
179	Add serde to your `Cargo.toml`:
180	
181	```toml
182	[dependencies]
183	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
184	```
185	
186	Update your types:
187	
188	```rust
189	use serde::Serialize;
190	
191	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
192	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
193	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
194	
195	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
196	pub struct Todo {
197	    pub title: String,
198	    pub status: Status,
199	}
200	
201	#[derive(Serialize)]
202	pub struct TodoResult {
203	    pub message: Option<String>,
204	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
205	}
206	```
207	
208	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
209	
210	## 4. Replace Imperative Print Statements With a Template
211	
212	Reading a template of an output next to the substituting variables is much easier to reason about than scattered prints, string concats and the like.
213	
214	This step is optional - if your current output is simple, you can skip to step 5. If you want an intermediate checkpoint, use Rust's format strings:
215	
216	```rust
217	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
218	    let output = format!(
219	        "{header}\n{todos}",
220	        header = result.message.unwrap_or_default(),
221	        todos = result.todos.iter().enumerate()
222	            .map(|(i, t)| format!("{}. [{}] {}", i + 1, t.status, t.title))
223	            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
224	            .join("\n")
225	    );
226	    println!("{}", output);
227	}
228	```
229	
230	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should still work.
231	
232	## 5. Use a MiniJinja Template String
233	
234	Rewrite your `std::fmt` or imperative prints into a MiniJinja template string, and add minijinja to your crate. If you're not familiar with it, it's a Rust implementation of Jinja, pretty much a de-facto standard for more complex templates.
235	
236	**Resources:**
237	
238	- [MiniJinja docs](https://docs.rs/minijinja)
239	- [Jinja syntax reference](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.1.x/templates/)
240	
241	Add minijinja to your `Cargo.toml`:
242	
243	```toml
244	[dependencies]
245	minijinja = "2"
246	```
247	
248	> **A note on booleans and none:** a bare `minijinja::Environment` renders these
249	> the Jinja2 way — `True`, `False`, `None` — from minijinja 2.22 onward.
250	> Standout renders `true`, `false`, and `none`, and normalizes for you from step
251	> 7 on, once rendering goes through `App`. Until then the spelling is
252	> minijinja's. If you want standout's spelling now, add `standout-render = "9"`
253	> next to minijinja and build the environment with
254	> `standout_render::template::new_environment()` instead of
255	> `minijinja::Environment::new()` in the snippets below — the snippets keep the
256	> bare constructor, since `standout` only arrives in step 7.
257	
258	And then you call render in MiniJinja, passing the template string and the data to use. So now your rendering function looks like this:
259	
260	```rust
261	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
262	    let output_tmpl = r#"
263	{% if message %}
264	    {{ message }}
265	{% endif %}
266	{% for todo in todos %}
267	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
268	{% endfor %}
269	"#;
270	
271	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
272	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(output_tmpl).unwrap();
273	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
274	    println!("{}", output);
275	}
276	```
277	
278	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should match (formatting may differ slightly).

280	## 6. Use a Dedicated Template File
281	
282	Now, move the template content into a file (say `src/templates/list.jinja`), and load it in the rendering module. Dedicated files have several advantages: triggering editor/IDE support for the file type, more descriptive diffs, less risk of breaking the code/build and, in the event that you have less technical people helping out with the UI, a much cleaner and simpler way for them to contribute.
283	
284	Create `src/templates/list.jinja`:
285	
286	```jinja
287	{% if message %}{{ message }} {% endif %}
288	{% for todo in todos %}
289	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
290	{% endfor %}
291	```

293	Update your render function to load from file:
294

297	    let template_content = include_str!("templates/list.jinja");
298	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
299	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(template_content).unwrap();
300	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
301	    println!("{}", output);
302	}

331	
332	And now the Standout-specific bits finally show up.
333	
334	### 7.1 Add Standout to your Cargo.toml
335	
336	```toml
337	[dependencies]
338	standout = "9"
339	anyhow = "1"
340	```
341	
342	A single `standout` dependency is enough: `standout` re-exports `standout-dispatch`
343	as `standout::dispatch`, and code generated by `#[handler]`, `Questionnaire`, and
344	`QuestionnaireChoices` resolves against whichever of the two crates your
345	`Cargo.toml` declares.
346	
347	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - dependencies should download and compile.

349	### 7.2 Create Handlers with the `#[handler]` Macro
350	
351	The `#[handler]` macro transforms typed Rust functions into Standout-compatible
352	handlers. Keep application behavior in the CLI-free core; the handler annotates
353	CLI parameters, calls the core, and maps its result into serializable view data.
354	
355	See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for full handler API details.
356	
357	```rust
358	use standout::cli::Output;
359	use standout::handler;
360	
361	mod handlers {
362	    use super::*;
363	
364	    // Thin CLI adapter - easy to test, no extraction boilerplate
365	    #[handler]
366	    pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
367	        let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
368	        let todos = core::list(filter)?;
369	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
370	    }
371	
372	    #[handler]
373	    pub fn add(#[arg] title: String) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
374	        let todo = core::add(title)?;
375	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
376	            message: Some(format!("Added: {}", todo.title)),
377	            todos: vec![todo],
378	        }))
379	    }
380	}
381	```
382	
383	The `#[handler]` macro:
384	
385	- Extracts CLI arguments automatically from `ArgMatches`
386	- Converts `#[flag]` to `bool` flags, `#[arg]` to required/optional args
387	- Auto-wraps `Result<T, E>` in `Output::Render` for you
388	
389	**Parameter Annotations:**
390	
391	| Annotation | Type | What it extracts |
392	| ------------ | ------ | ------------------ |
393	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | Boolean flag (`--verbose`) |
394	| `#[arg]` | `T` | Required argument |
395	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | Optional argument |
396	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | Multiple values |
397	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | Access to context (when needed) |
398	
399	### 7.2.1 Connect Commands to Handlers
400	
401	```rust
402	use clap::Subcommand;
403	use standout::cli::Dispatch;
404	
405	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
406	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
407	pub enum Commands {
408	    #[dispatch(pure)]
409	    List {
410	        #[arg(short, long)]
411	        all: bool,
412	    },
413	    #[dispatch(pure)]
414	    Add {
415	        title: String,
416	    },
417	}
418	```
419	
420	The derive macro matches each variant to a handler function by its kebab-case
421	command name (`List` registers as `list`). With `#[dispatch(pure)]`, the
422	variant resolves to the wrapper `#[handler]` generated for the function —
423	`List` → `handlers::list__handler`. Without `pure`, the variant calls
424	`handlers::list` directly, and that function must already have the
425	`fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>` dispatch signature.
426	
427	The `Dispatch` derive connects a variant to a handler; it does not declare the
428	variant's arguments. Those stay clap's, so each variant keeps the fields its
429	handler's `#[flag]` and `#[arg]` parameters read — `all` for `list`, `title`
430	for `add` — exactly as in the plain-clap version at the top of this guide.
431	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports a handler asking for an argument the
432	variant does not declare, which otherwise surfaces as a `get_flag` panic at
433	run time.
434	
435	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
436	
437	### 7.2.2 Accessing App State (Optional)
438	
439	When your handler needs shared resources like databases, use the `#[ctx]` annotation:
440	
441	```rust
442	#[handler]
443	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
444	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
445	    let todos = db.list()?;
446	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
447	}
448	```
449	
450	> **Note:** For the full handler signature (without macros) and advanced patterns, see [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md).

486	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;

494	### 7.4 Wire up main()
495	
496	The final bit: handling the dispatching off to Standout:
497	
498	```rust
499	use standout::cli::App;
500	use standout::embed_templates;
501	
502	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
503	    let app = App::builder()
504	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
505	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
506	        .build()?;
507	
508	    // Run with auto dispatch - handles parsing and execution
509	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
510	    Ok(())
511	}
512	```
513	
514	If your app has other clap commands that are not managed by Standout, check for unhandled commands. See [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for details on incremental migration.
515	
516	```rust
517	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
518	    // Standout didn't handle this command, fall back to legacy.
519	    legacy_dispatch();
520	}
521	```
522	
523	If the fallback needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`, call `run_with` with a
524	detected target and input sources, then match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`
525	on `into_outcome()`:
526	
527	```rust
528	let target = standout::TargetProperties::detect();
529	let sources = standout::InputSources::from_process();
530	let result = app.run_with(Cli::command(), std::env::args(), target, sources);
531	match result.into_outcome() {
532	    standout::cli::DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches) => legacy_dispatch(matches),
533	    _ => {}
534	}
535	```
536	
537	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - it should work as before.
538	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list --output json` - you should get JSON output for free!
539	
540	And now you can remove the boilerplate: the orchestrator (`list_command`) and
541	the rendering (`render_list`). A single derive attribute links each CLI handler
542	adapter to a command name, a few lines configure Standout, and auto dispatch
543	handles the shell boilerplate.
544	
545	For the next commands you migrate, add a thin adapter plus its template. By
546	default the macro matches the command's name to handlers and template files,
547	but you can map either explicitly.

698	## Bonus: Pipe Output to External Commands
699	
700	Need to filter output through `jq`, log to a file with `tee`, or copy to clipboard? Standout supports piping rendered output to external commands:
701	
702	```rust
703	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
704	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
705	pub enum Commands {
706	    /// List todos, extracting just titles with jq
707	    #[dispatch(pipe_through = "jq '.todos[].title'")]
708	    List,
709	
710	    /// Export todos to clipboard
711	    #[dispatch(pipe_to_clipboard)]
712	    Export,
713	}
714	```
715	
716	Or via the builder API. `#[handler]` generates a unit struct named after the
717	function with a capitalized suffix (`list` → `list_Handler`) that implements
718	`Handler` directly; register that struct — the plain `handlers::list` function
719	is not itself registrable — with `command_with`:
720	
721	```rust
722	let app = App::builder()
723	    .command_with("list", handlers::list_Handler, |cfg| {
724	        cfg.template_name("list")
725	           .pipe_through("jq '.todos'")  // Filter JSON output
726	    })?
727	    .command_with("export", handlers::export_Handler, |cfg| {
728	        cfg.template_name("export")
729	           .pipe_to("tee /tmp/export.log")  // Log while displaying
730	           .pipe_to_clipboard()  // Then copy to clipboard
731	    })?
732	    .build()?;
733	```
734	
735	Three piping modes:
736	
737	- `pipe_through("cmd")`: Use command's stdout as new output (filters like jq, sort)
738	- `pipe_to("cmd")`: Run command but keep original output (side effects like tee)
739	- `pipe_to_clipboard()`: Send to system clipboard (pbcopy on macOS, xclip on Linux)
740	
741	See [Output Piping](../crates/pipe/topics/piping.md) for the full API.
742	
743	## Bonus: Declarative Input Collection
744	
745	Need to accept input from CLI arguments, piped stdin, environment variables, or interactive prompts? `standout-input` provides declarative input chains, and the `App` builder integrates them as a first-class part of command configuration:
746	
747	```rust
748	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContextInput, FnHandler, Output};
749	use standout::input::{ArgSource, EditorSource, EnvSource, InputChain, StdinSource};
750	
751	App::builder()
752	    .command_with("create", FnHandler::new(create), |cfg| {
753	        cfg.template_name("create")
754	            .input("body", InputChain::<String>::new()
755	                .try_source(ArgSource::new("body"))           // 1. --body argument
756	                .try_source(StdinSource::new())                // 2. Piped stdin
757	                .try_source(EnvSource::new("PR_BODY"))         // 3. Environment variable
758	                .try_source(EditorSource::new().extension(".md"))  // 4. Open editor
759	                .validate(|s| !s.is_empty(), "Body cannot be empty"))
760	    })?
761	    .build()?;
762	
763	fn create(_m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Value> {
764	    // The chain has already been resolved before the handler runs.
765	    let body: &String = ctx.input("body")?;
766	    /* business logic ... */
767	}
768	```
769	
770	Features:
771	
772	- **Declarative priority**: Source order is explicit in the chain
773	- **Framework-integrated**: `.input(name, chain)` registers the chain alongside `template`, `hooks`, and `pipe_*`; resolution happens in pre-dispatch
774	- **Testable**: All sources accept mocks for CI-safe testing (the `TestHarness` from `standout-test` wires them automatically)
775	- **Validated**: Chain-level validation with retry support for interactive sources
776	- **Feature-gated**: Control dependencies (editor, prompts, inquire TUI)
777	
778	The chain still works standalone via `chain.resolve(&matches)?` for cases where input shape depends on already-resolved values.
779	
780	See [Introduction to Input](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) and [Framework Integration](../crates/input/topics/framework-integration.md) for the full guide.
781	
782	Aside from exposing the library primitives, Standout leverages best-in-breed crates like MiniJinja and console::Style under the hood. The lock-in is really negligible: you can use Standout's BB parser or swap it, manually dispatch handlers, and use the renderers directly in your clap dispatch.
783	
784	## Mutable Handlers
785	
786	A closure passed to `command_with` runs as `FnMut`, so it can capture and
787	mutate state directly — no `Arc<Mutex<_>>` wrappers needed. This is common
788	with database connections, file caches, or in-memory indices. Wrap the
789	closure in `FnHandler::new` so it implements `Handler`:
790	
791	```rust
792	use std::collections::HashMap;
793	
794	use clap::ArgMatches;
795	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, FnHandler, Output};
796	use standout::embed_templates;
797	use uuid::Uuid;
798	
799	struct PadStore {
800	    index: HashMap<Uuid, Metadata>,
801	}
802	
803	impl PadStore {
804	    fn complete(&mut self, id: Uuid) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
805	        // This needs &mut self
806	        self.index.get_mut(&id).unwrap().completed = true;
807	        Ok(())
808	    }
809	}
810	
811	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
812	    let mut store = PadStore::load()?;
813	
814	    App::builder()
815	        .app_state(Config::load()?)
816	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
817	        .command_with(
818	            "complete",
819	            FnHandler::new(|m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
820	                let id = m.get_one::<Uuid>("id").unwrap();
821	                store.complete(*id)?; // &mut store works!
822	                Ok(Output::Silent)
823	            }),
824	            |cfg| cfg.silent(),
825	        )?
826	        .command_with(
827	            "list",
828	            FnHandler::new(|_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
829	                Ok(Output::Render(store.list()))
830	            }),
831	            |cfg| cfg,
832	        )?
833	        .build()?
834	        .run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
835	    Ok(())
836	}
837	```
838	
839	**Handler capabilities:**
840	
841	- `command_with` accepts anything implementing `Handler`; `FnHandler::new`
842	  turns a plain `FnMut` closure into one
843	- Handlers can capture `&mut` references to state
844	- The `Handler` trait uses `&mut self` for struct-based handlers
845	- No `Send + Sync` requirements—CLI apps are single-threaded
846	
847	## Appendix: Common Errors and Troubleshooting
848	
849	- Template not found
850	  - **Error:** `template 'list' not found`
851	  - **Cause:** The template path in `embed_templates!` doesn't match your file structure.
852	  - **Fix:** Ensure the path is relative to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g., `embed_templates!("src/templates")` and that the file is named `list.jinja`, `list.j2`, or `list.txt`.
853	- Style not applied
854	  - **Symptom:** Text appears but without colors/formatting.
855	  - **Cause:** Style name in template doesn't match stylesheet.
856	  - **Fix:** Check that `[mystyle]` in your template matches `.mystyle` in CSS or `mystyle:` in YAML. Run with `--output term-debug` to see style tag names.
857	- Handler not called
858	  - **Symptom:** Command runs but nothing happens or wrong handler runs.
859	  - **Cause:** Command name mismatch between clap enum variant and handler function.
860	  - **Fix:** Ensure enum variant `List` maps to function `handlers::list` (snake_case conversion). Or use explicit mapping: `#[dispatch(handler = my_custom_handler)]`
861	- JSON output is empty or wrong
862	  - **Symptom:** `--output json` produces unexpected results.
863	  - **Cause:** `Serialize` derive is missing or field names don't match template expectations.
864	  - **Fix:** Ensure all types in your result implement `Serialize`. Use `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` for consistent naming.
865	- Styles not loading
866	  - **Error:** `theme not found: default`
867	  - **Cause:** Stylesheet file missing or wrong path.
868	  - **Fix:** Ensure `src/styles/default.css` exists. Check `embed_styles!` path matches your file structure.

1	# Execution Model
2	
3	`standout-dispatch` manages a strict linear pipeline from CLI input to rendered
4	output. This explicitly separated flow keeps handler adapters decoupled from
5	presentation (renderers) and shell pipeline side effects (hooks).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## The Pipeline
10	
11	```text
12	Clap Parsing → Pre-dispatch → Handler → Post-dispatch → Renderer → Post-output → Piping → Output
13	```
14	
15	Each stage has a clear responsibility:
16	
17	**Clap Parsing**: Your `clap::Command` definition is parsed normally. `standout-dispatch` doesn't replace clap—it works with the resulting `ArgMatches`.
18	
19	**Pre-dispatch Hook**: Runs before the handler. Can abort execution (e.g., auth checks).
20	
21	**Handler**: Your CLI adapter executes. It receives `ArgMatches` and
22	`CommandContext`, calls the CLI-free application library, and returns a
23	`HandlerResult<T>`—either data to render, a silent marker, or binary content.
24	For simpler adapters, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed functions that
25	return `Result<T, E>` directly (see [Handler Contract](handler-contract.md)).
26	
27	**Post-dispatch Hook**: Runs after the handler, before rendering. Can transform data.
28	
29	**Renderer**: Your render function receives the data and produces output (string or binary).
30	
31	**Post-output Hook**: Runs after rendering. Can transform the final output string.
32	
33	**Piping**: Optionally sends output to external commands (jq, tee, clipboard). Implemented as specialized post-output hooks. See [Output Piping](../../pipe/topics/piping.md).
34	
35	**Output**: The result is returned or written to stdout.
36	
37	---
38	
39	## Command Paths
40	
41	A command path is a vector of strings representing the subcommand chain:
42	
43	```bash
44	myapp db migrate --steps 5
45	```
46	
47	The command path is `["db", "migrate"]`.
48	
49	### Extracting Command Paths
50	
51	```rust
52	use standout_dispatch::{extract_command_path, path_to_string, get_deepest_matches};
53	
54	let matches = cmd.get_matches();
55	
56	// Get the full path
57	let path = extract_command_path(&matches);  // ["db", "migrate"]
58	
59	// Convert to dot notation
60	let path_str = path_to_string(&path);  // "db.migrate"
61	
62	// Get ArgMatches for the deepest command
63	let deep = get_deepest_matches(&matches);  // ArgMatches for "migrate"
64	```
65	
66	### Command Path Utilities
67	
68	| Function | Purpose |
69	| ---------- | --------- |
70	| `extract_command_path` | Get subcommand chain as `Vec<String>` |
71	| `path_to_string` | Convert path to dot notation (`"db.migrate"`) |
72	| `string_to_path` | Convert dot notation to path |
73	| `get_deepest_matches` | Get `ArgMatches` for deepest subcommand |
74	| `has_subcommand` | Check if any subcommand was invoked |
75	
76	---
77	
78	## State Injection
79	
80	Handlers access state through `CommandContext`, which provides two mechanisms:
81	
82	- **`app_state`**: Shared, immutable state configured at build time (database, config)
83	- **`extensions`**: Per-request, mutable state injected by hooks
84	
85	```rust
86	fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
87	    // App state: shared resources
88	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
89	
90	    // Extensions: per-request state
91	    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;
92	    // ...
93	}
94	```
95	
96	> For full details on state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
97	
98	---
99	
100	## The Hooks System
101	
102	Hooks are functions that run at specific points in the pipeline. They let you intercept, validate, or transform without touching handler logic—keeping concerns separated.
103	
104	### Three Phases
105	
106	**Pre-dispatch**: Runs before the handler. Can abort execution or inject per-request state.
107	
108	Use for: authentication checks, input validation, logging start time, **injecting per-request state** via `extensions`.
109	
110	Pre-dispatch hooks receive `&mut CommandContext`, allowing them to inject state via `ctx.extensions` that handlers can retrieve. They also have read access to `ctx.app_state` for shared resources:
111	
112	```rust
113	use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};
114	
115	// Per-request state types (injected by hooks)
116	struct UserSession { user_id: u64 }
117	
118	Hooks::new()
119	    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
120	        // Read from app_state (shared)
121	        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
122	
123	        // Validate and set up per-request state
124	        let token = std::env::var("API_TOKEN")
125	            .map_err(|_| HookError::pre_dispatch("API_TOKEN required"))?;
126	
127	        let user_id = db.validate_token(&token)?;
128	
129	        // Inject into extensions (per-request)
130	        ctx.extensions.insert(UserSession { user_id });
131	        Ok(())
132	    })
133	```
134	
135	Handlers then use both app_state and extensions:
136	
137	```rust
138	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
139	    // App state: shared across all requests
140	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
141	
142	    // Extensions: per-request state from hooks
143	    let session = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserSession>()?;
144	
145	    let items = db.fetch_items(session.user_id)?;
146	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
147	}
148	```
149	
150	See [App State and Extensions](app-state.md#extensions-per-request-state) for the `Extensions` API and the two-state model.
151	
152	**Post-dispatch**: Runs after the handler, before rendering. Can transform data.
153	
154	Use for: adding timestamps, filtering sensitive fields, data enrichment. The hook receives handler output as `serde_json::Value`, allowing generic transformations regardless of the handler's output type.
155	
156	```rust
157	Hooks::new().post_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx, mut data| {
158	    if let Some(obj) = data.as_object_mut() {
159	        obj.insert("generated_at".into(), json!(Utc::now().to_rfc3339()));
160	    }
161	    Ok(data)
162	})
163	```
164	
165	**Post-output**: Runs after rendering. Can transform the final string.
166	
167	Use for: adding headers/footers, logging, metrics. The hook receives `RenderedOutput`—an enum of `Text(TextOutput)`, `Binary(Vec<u8>, String)`, `Artifact(ArtifactOutput)`, or `Silent`. For an artifact the bytes and report are still pre-write, so a hook may transform them via `as_artifact_mut()`; the framework, not the hook, performs the final write.
168	
169	```rust
170	use standout_dispatch::RenderedOutput;
171	
172	Hooks::new().post_output(|_matches, _ctx, output| {
173	    match output {
174	        RenderedOutput::Text(s) => {
175	            Ok(RenderedOutput::Text(format!("{}\n-- Generated by MyApp", s)))
176	        }
177	        other => Ok(other),
178	    }
179	})
180	```
181	
182	### Hook Chaining
183	
184	Multiple hooks per phase are supported. Pre-dispatch hooks run sequentially—first error aborts. Post-dispatch and post-output hooks *chain*: each receives the output of the previous, enabling composable transformations.
185	
186	```rust
187	Hooks::new()
188	    .post_dispatch(add_metadata)      // Runs first
189	    .post_dispatch(filter_sensitive)  // Receives add_metadata's output
190	```
191	
192	Order matters: `filter_sensitive` sees the metadata that `add_metadata` inserted.
193	
194	### Output Piping
195	
196	Piping sends rendered output to external shell commands. It's implemented as specialized post-output hooks with three modes:
197	
198	```rust
199	use standout::cli::App;
200	
201	let app = App::builder()
202	    .commands(|g| {
203	        g.command_with("export", handlers::export, |cfg| {
204	            cfg.template_name("export")
205	               // Filter through jq (capture mode)
206	               .pipe_through("jq '.items'")
207	        })
208	        .command_with("copy", handlers::copy, |cfg| {
209	            cfg.template_name("copy")
210	               // Send to clipboard (consume mode)
211	               .pipe_to_clipboard()
212	        })
213	        .command_with("debug", handlers::debug, |cfg| {
214	            cfg.template_name("debug")
215	               // Log to file while displaying (passthrough mode)
216	               .pipe_to("tee /tmp/debug.log")
217	        })
218	    })
219	    .build()?;
220	```
221	
222	| Mode | Method | Behavior |
223	| ------ | -------- | ---------- |
224	| Passthrough | `pipe_to()` | Run command, return original output |
225	| Capture | `pipe_through()` | Return command's stdout as new output |
226	| Consume | `pipe_to_clipboard()` | Send to clipboard, return empty |
227	
228	Pipes can be chained and combined with other post-output hooks. See [Output Piping](../../pipe/topics/piping.md) for full documentation.
229	
230	### Error Handling
231	
232	When a hook returns `Err(HookError)`:
233	
234	- Execution stops immediately
235	- Remaining hooks in that phase don't run
236	- For pre-dispatch: the handler never executes
237	- For post phases: the rendered output is discarded
238	- The error message is returned
239	
240	```rust
241	use standout_dispatch::HookError;
242	
243	// Create error with phase context
244	HookError::pre_dispatch("database connection failed")
245	
246	// With source error for debugging
247	HookError::post_dispatch("transformation failed")
248	    .with_source(underlying_error)
249	```
250	
251	---
252	
253	## Default Command Support
254	
255	Handle the case when no subcommand is specified:
256	
257	```rust
258	use standout_dispatch::{has_subcommand, insert_default_command};
259	
260	let matches = cmd.get_matches_from(args);
261	
262	if !has_subcommand(&matches) {
263	    // Re-parse with default command inserted
264	    let args_with_default = insert_default_command(std::env::args(), "list");
265	    let matches = cmd.get_matches_from(args_with_default);
266	    // Now dispatch to "list"
267	}
268	```
269	
270	`insert_default_command` inserts the command name after the binary name but before any flags.
271	
272	---
273	
274	## Putting It Together
275	
276	A complete dispatch flow:
277	
278	```rust
279	use standout_dispatch::{
280	    SimpleFnHandler, FnHandler, Output, CommandContext, Hooks, HookError,
281	    extract_command_path, get_deepest_matches, path_to_string,
282	};
283	
284	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
285	    // 1. Define clap command
286	    let cmd = Command::new("myapp")
287	        .subcommand(Command::new("list"))
288	        .subcommand(Command::new("delete").arg(Arg::new("id").required(true)));
289	
290	    // 2. Create handlers
291	    // SimpleFnHandler: for handlers that don't need CommandContext
292	    let list_handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|_m| {
293	        storage::list()  // Result<T, E> auto-wraps in Output::Render
294	    });
295	
296	    // FnHandler: when you need CommandContext
297	    let delete_handler = FnHandler::new(|matches, _ctx| {
298	        let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
299	        storage::delete(id)?;
300	        Ok(Output::Silent)
301	    });
302	
303	    // 3. Create hooks
304	    let hooks = Hooks::new()
305	        .pre_dispatch(|_m, _ctx| {
306	            println!("Starting command...");
307	            Ok(())
308	        });
309	
310	    // 4. Parse and dispatch
311	    let matches = cmd.get_matches();
312	    let path = extract_command_path(&matches);
313	    let mut ctx = CommandContext {
314	        command_path: path.clone(),
315	        ..Default::default()
316	    };
317	
318	    // Run pre-dispatch hooks (may inject state via ctx.extensions)
319	    hooks.run_pre_dispatch(&matches, &mut ctx)?;
320	
321	    // Dispatch based on command
322	    let result = match path_to_string(&path).as_str() {
323	        "list" => {
324	            let output = list_handler.handle(&matches, &ctx)?;
325	            if let Output::Render(data) = output {
326	                println!("{}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&data)?);
327	            }
328	        }
329	        "delete" => {
330	            let deep = get_deepest_matches(&matches);
331	            delete_handler.handle(deep, &ctx)?;
332	            println!("Deleted.");
333	        }
334	        _ => eprintln!("Unknown command"),
335	    };
336	
337	    Ok(())
338	}
339	```
340	
341	---
342	
343	## Summary
344	
345	The execution model provides:
346	
347	1. **Clear pipeline** — Each stage has defined inputs and outputs
348	2. **Hook points** — Intercept before, after handler, and after render
349	3. **Command routing** — Utilities for navigating subcommand hierarchies
350	4. **Presentation ownership** — Rendering stays outside dispatch handlers
351	5. **Testable stages** — Each component can be tested in isolation
352
